title: If a Tree Falls in the Wilderness, Will We Hear (About) It?
author: Katie Bilodeau
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Washakie-
Wilderness-Wyoming-by-Howie-
Wolke.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/21/if-a-tree-falls-in-the-
wilderness-will-we-hear-about-it/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Washakie-
Wilderness-Wyoming-by-Howie-Wolke.jpg)

Washakie Wilderness, Shoshone National Forest, Wyoming. Photo: Howie Wolke.

The U.S. Forest Service has approved a tree-cutting project in the Washakie
Wilderness in Wyoming behind closed doors. Does it promote a wilderness ethic?
Certainly not. Will it violate the Wilderness Act? Most likely. Will the
public know the full details about this project before it is complete?
Unlikely. Should the Forest Service still hear from you on this? YES,
ABSOLUTELY.

There are two parts to this story. The first is the utter absurdity of the
project itself. The second is how the Forest Service cut the public out of any
notice or engagement. You should be furious at both—I am.

Last month one of our fellow conservation groups alerted us about a Forest
Service project in the Shoshone National Forest’s Washakie Wilderness to cut
down a tree. At that point, just about the only information available
originated from a [news
article](https://default.salsalabs.org/T0a8b51b9-18fe-4bb2-a43d-6f72aa24ffcd/dc319890-760f-4844-8257-ece3092b6f52)
about the Wyoming state legislature’s debate on funding this project.

The Forest Service approved a project to cut down a tree and helicopter it out
of a protected Wilderness so it may stand in a museum and remind us that we
should preserve—and not log—our federal lands. Kind of like paving paradise to
put up a parking lot, but then adding an interpretive sign describing the
paradise that once existed.

What motivates this project? A survey crew stranded in a snowstorm 133 years
ago carved their names into a tree outside of Yellowstone National Park. The
survey crew was marking the Yellowstone Forest Reserve in early efforts to
preserve forests instead of logging them. That forest reserve eventually
became the Shoshone National Forest. The Washakie Wilderness was later
established with the original passing of the 1964 Wilderness Act. Congress
expanded this Wilderness in 1972, and then again in 1984. The survey tree is
within the Washakie Wilderness—over two dozen miles from the nearest
trailhead.

The survey crew might have even been proud that what they sought to preserve
was ultimately protected by our strongest environmental law. But they didn’t
count on others valuing their carvings over actual wilderness preservation.

When I connected with the Forest Service project lead on July 31, 2026, he
confirmed that the plan was to go into the Wilderness to cut down and remove
this tree. The Forest Service had decided a couple weeks before that to do the
project under a categorical exclusion. He told me that they had already cut
out trees and brushed out a user-created trail to get to this tree. Flooding
had blown out a trail, delaying their project, but on August 7, 2026, a state-
contracted crew would haul equipment in on this new trail to image this tree
for historic preservation purposes. Then, the project lead said, the plan was
to go back in, cut the tree down, and helicopter it out of the Wilderness
later this year when a slowing fire season freed up a helicopter. Neither of
these later two action items have dates, though they seem imminent. The tree
would be displayed in a museum to tell the story of our public lands.

On August 4, 2026, Wilderness Watch sent the project lead and the Shoshone
National Forest Supervisor Ken Coffin [a
letter](https://default.salsalabs.org/T9a4f8ed2-00d7-4fb7-9add-
afb893127882/dc319890-760f-4844-8257-ece3092b6f52) asking the Forest Service
to delay this project until the agency could meaningfully engage the public.
The Forest Service hadn’t notified the public of this project—it wasn’t even
listed as a project on their website when I went looking for it in July. We
reminded Supervisor Coffin that the Forest Service’s primary obligation in
administering Wilderness is to protect wilderness character, which includes
“preservation and protection in their natural condition.” To the extent that
the Wilderness Act allows narrow administrative exceptions for prohibited
tools, it’s only when necessary to further the purpose of the act: an enduring
wilderness resource for future generations. We noted that this project has no
wilderness purpose.

We asked for the Forest Service to minimally pause this project until they at
least meaningfully engage interested folks and organizations in a public
process.

Supervisor Coffin emailed back on August 13, 2026, declining our request. Even
though the U.S. Department of Agriculture has current regulations that allow
the agency to engage the public on projects, Supervisor Coffin’s response
email indicated that he intended to move forward without public input because
it wasn’t “required.” He said he believed that this project would “benefit”
Wilderness because telling a story about public lands achieved the “greater
good,” particularly, “why it’s important for us to hold [public land] in the
highest regard now and into the future.”

Does 1) building a non-system trail in Wilderness; 2) cutting down trees in
Wilderness to access this “survey” tree; 3) cutting down that tree, which is
well over a century old; and 4) helicoptering it out of Wilderness hold our
most protected places in the “highest regard now and into the future?” Or is
this human folly? The names that were carved into this tree 133 years ago were
carved into a tree  _that was big enough to carve names into it 133 years
ago_. Dead or alive, this tree (and the others cut down to access it), could
have been preserved and protected in its natural condition within the
Wilderness. This survey tree and the space around it might have been, still
are, or might become home to a community of life larger than our human sphere.
Keeping the tree where it is—and saying no to whoever had this truly perverse
idea—is how we act to hold Wilderness in the highest regard now and into the
future.

This past summer, I visited a famous site for Ediacaran fossils in
Newfoundland. Ediacaran fossils existed over 540 million years ago—when life
transitioned from single cell to multi-cell organisms. It was life before
dinosaurs. These fossils, on slabs of rocks right next to the Atlantic, are
slowly eroding away. But instead of drilling them off of their rocks and
putting them in a museum, archeologists took a cast for replicas, and will
allow people to enjoy it  _in situ_ while nature takes its course. If the
Province of Newfoundland can do that for ancient fossils, surely there are
alternatives that the State of Wyoming could suggest to the current course so
133-year-old carvings can be preserved without removing the tree from the
Washakie Wilderness?

There is a lot we don’t know about the project, and this is the much shorter
second part to this story. When will they cut the tree? How many miles of work
did the Forest Service allow on a non-system trail in Wilderness and how
intensive was that trail work? Did they use chainsaws? Are chainsaws involved
in plans moving forward? Do they have to land a helicopter in the Wilderness
to remove the tree? Do they have to cut down more trees in the Wilderness for
a helicopter landing pad?

I submitted a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request for decision documents
on July 30, 2026, the day before the Forest Service project leader called me
back. I asked for “expedited processing” because there was so much the public
doesn’t know about a project that is imminent. If granted, it would have
shortened the response time to 10 days instead of the statutorily mandated 20,
and we would have had the documents by August 13. When I spoke with the
project leader, he indicated the Forest Service had done a “minimum
requirements analysis” and considered that their decision document. Even
though the project leader referenced their decision document, which presumably
is at their fingertips and an easy “search” for a responsive record, even
though the forest supervisor received a copy of my targeted FOIA request the
same day I submitted it, and even though the supervisor responded to
Wilderness Watch’s letter that they wouldn’t engage the public,  _the Forest
Service has yet to provide this decision document_.

There can be a third part to this story—it’s one I hope our members and
supporters write. The Shoshone National Forest Supervisor and project lead
should hear from you. Though they have not sought public involvement, the
public should involve itself. This must have been someone’s pet project, and
the Forest Service circumvented all of us to accomplish it. This is not unlike
going behind the public’s back [to let outfitters loose with chainsaws in
Wilderness](https://default.salsalabs.org/T394f7b4e-e77e-42ff-a5ff-d906106c5cbd/dc319890-760f-4844-8257-ece3092b6f52),
[allowing permanent private cabins to persist in
Wilderness](https://default.salsalabs.org/T89980d03-c58b-4786-85d9-3d08f8d73aa2/dc319890-760f-4844-8257-ece3092b6f52),
or finding vacant grazing allotments in Wilderness that are recovering and
[permitting the reintroduction of cows at the behest of
ranchers](https://default.salsalabs.org/T870d7b32-20b8-4caf-8965-df022b15a9f9/dc319890-760f-4844-8257-ece3092b6f52)
without notifying or engaging the public. All of these developments are
happening right now. Though it’s not selling off your public lands, it is the
agency’s alternative plan—letting private interests have their way with
Wilderness without the public’s knowledge or involvement.

Please email the Shoshone National Forest supervisor and copy the project lead
for this survey tree.

Shoshone National Forest Supervisor, Ken Coffin:
[kenneth.coffin@usda.gov](https://default.salsalabs.org/T761a4429-c53d-4ec1-a09f-17a91aaf8eb8/dc319890-760f-4844-8257-ece3092b6f52)

Shoshone National Forest Project Lead, Mike LaFrentz:
[robert.lafrentz@usda.gov](https://default.salsalabs.org/Td9ca252a-1375-4cfa-9003-213a0913dbb1/dc319890-760f-4844-8257-ece3092b6f52)

Ask them to delay the project and engage the public. Also, tell them what you
think about this project based on the limited information available, and ask
for them to publish the decision document and any other analysis they
conducted. Let the public employees who administer your Wilderness know that
this doesn’t hold America’s wilderness heritage in high regard, and you don’t
appreciate the clandestine way the Forest Service handled this project.

Wilderness deserves better.
